[@aosp-selinux]SELinux – MAC binds even root; confinement limits a compromise's reach
Paper claims
  • Sec. 3 →SELinux confines even uid-0 processes to permitted domains.
  • Sec. 2 →SELinux confinement contains a compromise – it protects and confines system services and reduces the effects of malicious software, so one component's compromise does not yield the whole system.

"Android uses Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) to enforce mandatory access control (MAC) over all processes, even processes running with root/superuser privileges (Linux capabilities)."

Confines services, reduces malware's reach Android can better protect and confine system services, control access to application data and system logs, reduce the effects of malicious software, and protect users from potential flaws in code on mobile devices.

Android Open Source Project, Security-Enhanced Linux in Android.

[@aosp-file-based-encryption]File-based encryption – mandatory since Android 10; keys protected in hardware (TEE)
Paper claims
  • Sec. 7, 11 →FBE mandatory on devices launched with Android 10+, available since Android 7.
  • Sec. 2 →FBE encryption keys are protected by Keymaster/KeyMint in a Trusted Execution Environment – the key is bound to dedicated hardware.

"Android 7.0 and higher supports file-based encryption (FBE)." / "All devices launching with Android 10 and higher are required to use file-based encryption."

Keys bound to the TEE (dedicated hardware) KeyMint/Keymaster and Gatekeeper must be implemented in a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) to provide protection for the DE keys so that an unauthorized OS (custom OS flashed onto the device) cannot simply request the DE keys.

[@grapheneos-auditor]GrapheneOS Auditor – hardware-backed remote attestation from a second device
Paper claims
  • Sec. 12 →GrapheneOS provides hardware-backed remote attestation an owner can verify from a second device.
  • Sec. 12 →The released Auditor recognizes only verified-boot keys compiled into it; for a self-signed (alternate-OS) state these are the official GrapheneOS keys, so an owner's self-generated verified-boot key is not recognized, and an owner-signed build needs an owner-configured Auditor and Attestation Server.

"The Auditor app uses hardware-based security features to validate the identity of a device, along with the authenticity and integrity of the operating system. It ensures the device is running a verified operating system with a locked bootloader and that no tampering has occurred." / "Any device with Android 13 or higher can run the Auditor app and use it to verify other devices. However, only devices launched with Android 8.0 or later have the necessary hardware support for being verified."

Released app recognizes only compiled-in keys Alternative operating systems need their verified boot key included in the Auditor app and Attestation Server.

attestation.app/about; corroborated in Auditor source AttestationProtocol.java – the self-signed branch pins only official GrapheneOS keys and rejects any unpinned verified-boot key.

[@grapheneos-auditor-domain]Auditor source – the attestation server domain is hardcoded

[@magisk-details]Magisk – patched init runs first and shapes the SELinux policy it then runs under
Paper claimSec. 8 →

modern root is control of init: the patched init runs before the SELinux policy is loaded (init loads it in userspace via security_load_policy, which magiskinit LD_PRELOAD-hooks), so the installer authors the policy its own daemon runs under (an unconstrained, permissive domain) rather than being confined by it – an administrative-tier initramfs modification, not an enlargement of in-system root.

"magiskinit replaces init as the first program to run." / "Sets LD_PRELOAD (init-ld) on init to hook security_load_policy" / "An unconstrained, permissive domain that magiskd and all root shells run in."

[@aosp-dm-verity]AOSP dm-verity – editing /system fails verification (why systemless)
Paper claimSec. 8 →

dm-verity is the integrity mechanism protecting /system (a hashtree); verified boot covers /system and boot/init_boot alike, so neither is editable on a locked device. dm-verity plus read-only EROFS/super make /system a harder, read-only target than the single flashable boot image – a secondary reason the method patches boot, not because boot is unprotected.

[@aosp-avb-readme]Android Verified Boot 2.0 – vbmeta-signature check, hashtree-disabled flag, owner-key YELLOW
Paper claimSec. 13 →

a vbmeta hashtree-disabled flag turns off dm-verity while the vbmeta still verifies under the owner's key, so the device boots locked (YELLOW state); the bootloader verifies the vbmeta signature, not the verity policy the signed vbmeta declares.

Bootloader verifies the vbmeta signature it starts by loading the vbmeta partition, checks the signature, and then goes on to load the boot partition for verification.

Owner-set key, locked -> YELLOW yellow: If in LOCKED state and the key used for verification was set by the end user.

Paper claimSec. 13 →

hardware-backed content protection (Widevine's top security level) depends on the device's trusted execution environment, a precondition that rests on the verified, vendor-keyed device state.

the same verified, vendor-keyed device state is a precondition for hardware-backed content protection: all Widevine levels require a signed system image loaded by a secure bootloader, and the hardware levels require the TEE components in the bootloader chain of trust.

Signed image + secure bootloader is a precondition All Widevine security levels require signed system images to be loaded on devices by a secure bootloader.
